claim: The dorsal periaqueductal gray (dPAG) controls defensive behaviors.
source: The dorsal periaqueductal gray (dPAG) controls defensive behaviors, but it is unknown how it represents states associated with threat approach and avoidance.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established knowledge about dPAG function.

claim: A dPAG threat-avoidance ensemble showed higher activity farther from threats such as the open arms of the elevated plus maze and a predator.
source: We identified a dPAG threatavoidance ensemble in mice that showed higher activity farther from threats such as the open arms of the elevated plus maze and a predator.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract based on experimental observations.

claim: Threat-avoidance ensemble cells were more active during threat avoidance behaviors such as escape and freezing.
source: These cells were also more active during threat avoidance behaviors such as escape and freezing, even though these behaviors have antagonistic motor output.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study reported in the abstract.

claim: Escape and freezing behaviors have antagonistic motor output.
source: These cells were also more active during threat avoidance behaviors such as escape and freezing, even though these behaviors have antagonistic motor output.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about these behaviors.

claim: The threat approach ensemble was more active during risk assessment behaviors and near threats.
source: Conversely, the threat approach ensemble was more active during risk assessment behaviors and near threats.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract.

claim: Unsupervised methods showed that avoidance/approach states were encoded with shared activity patterns across threats.
source: Furthermore, unsupervised methods showed that avoidance/approach states were encoded with shared activity patterns across threats.
evidence: This is a finding from computational analysis reported in the abstract.

claim: The relative number of cells in each ensemble predicted threat avoidance across mice.
source: Lastly, the relative number of cells in each ensemble predicted threat avoidance across mice.
evidence: This is a finding reported in the abstract based on analysis across animals.

claim: dPAG ensembles dynamically encode threat approach and avoidance states.
source: Thus, dPAG ensembles dynamically encode threat approach and avoidance states, providing a flexible mechanism to balance risk assessment and danger avoidance.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Behavioral variables and emotional states are thought to be represented in neural activity.
source: Behavioral variables and emotional states are thought to be represented in neural activity (for review, see Salzman and Fusi, 2010; Anderson and Adolphs, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: Neural representations must be specific enough to differentiate across behaviors, yet general enough to maintain functional cohesion across diverse threatening situations.
source: Such representations must be specific enough to differentiate across behaviors, yet general enough to maintain functional cohesion across diverse threatening situations (Gründemann et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: dPAG activity correlates with escape and freeze behaviors.
source: A large body of evidence has shown that defensive behaviors related to threat exposure are represented in dorsal periaqueductal gray (dPAG) activity (Deng et al., 2016; Esteban Masferrer et al., 2020; Evans et al., 2018; Watson et al., 2016), as dPAG activity correlates with escape and freeze.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior studies.

claim: dPAG optogenetic and electrical stimulation induce escape and freeze behaviors, as well as aversion.
source: Additionally, dPAG optogenetic and electrical stimulation induce these behaviors, as well as aversion (Brandão et al., 1982; Carvalho et al., 2015; Carvalho et al., 2018; Deng et al., 2016; Tovote et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior experimental studies.

claim: Pharmacological manipulations of dPAG activity impact open arm exploration in the elevated plus maze.
source: Furthermore, pharmacological manipulations of dPAG activity impact open arm exploration in the elevated plus maze (EPM), a traditional measure of rodent anxiety (Fogaça et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: PAG activity in humans correlates positively with threat imminence.
source: Lastly, PAG activity in humans correlates positively with threat imminence (Mobbs et al., 2007; Mobbs et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to human neuroimaging studies.

claim: The dPAG is a central node orchestrating defensive responses.
source: These reports show that the dPAG is a central node orchestrating defensive responses.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited literature.

claim: The two main behavioral states observed during exposure to threats are approach and avoidance.
source: The two main behavioral states observed during exposure to threats are approach and avoidance (Stankowich, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: In the approach state, animals voluntarily go near the threat and perform risk assessment behaviors.
source: In the approach state, animals voluntarily go near the threat and perform risk assessment behaviors.
evidence: This is a definition based on established behavioral concepts.

claim: In the approach state, the exploratory risk evaluation drive is stronger than the motivation to avoid danger.
source: In this state, the exploratory risk evaluation drive is stronger than the motivation to avoid danger.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the approach state based on behavioral theory.

claim: In the avoidance state, animals perceive high risk and attempt to minimize exposure to danger by escaping, freezing, and maintaining distance to the threat.
source: By contrast, in the avoidance state, animals perceive high risk, and thus attempt to minimize exposure to danger by escaping, freezing, and maintaining distance to the threat.
evidence: This is a definition based on established behavioral concepts.

claim: No reports to date have investigated whether the dPAG consistently encodes approach and avoidance states across distinct threats.
source: No reports to date have investigated whether the dPAG consistently encodes approach and avoidance states across distinct threats.
evidence: This identifies a gap in the literature that the current study addresses.

claim: 107 ± 19 cells per mouse were recorded during the EPM test (n = 8 mice; 857 cells total).
source: During the EPM test, we recorded 107 ± 19 cells per mouse (n = 8 mice; 857 cells were imaged; see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental data.

claim: Mice spent more time in the closed arms of the EPM than in the open arms.
source: As expected, mice spent more time in the closed arms of the EPM (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is reported in the text and shown in Figure 1B with statistical significance (W = 0, p=0.012).

claim: Mice displayed exploratory head dips over the edges of the open arms with an average frequency of 27.0 ± 9.7 events.
source: They also displayed exploratory head dips (average frequency of events = 27.0 ± 9.7; n = 8 mice) over the edges of the open arms (Figure 1B–C).
evidence: This is a direct report of behavioral data with reference to figures.

claim: During EPM exploration, cells often showed preferential activity either in closed or open arms.
source: During EPM exploration cells often showed preferential activity either in closed or open arms (Figure 1D–E).
evidence: This is reported in the text and illustrated in Figure 1D-E.

claim: The arm score distribution in the observed data is wider than expected by chance, indicating that dPAG cells show robust preference for EPM arm types.
source: The arm score distribution in the observed data is wider than expected by chance, indicating that dPAG cells show robust preference for EPM arm types (Figure 1F, left panel).
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis comparing observed to shuffled data.

claim: Cells fired similarly in arms of the same type, as cell activity in one open arm was highly correlated to activity in the other open arm.
source: The results showed that cells fired similarly in arms of the same type, as cell activity in one open arm was highly correlated to activity in the other open arm (Figure 1G, top panel).
evidence: This is a finding from correlation analysis shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Cell activity in closed and open arms was negatively correlated.
source: Conversely, cell activity in closed and open arms was negatively correlated (Figure 1G, bottom panel).
evidence: This is a finding from correlation analysis shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Roughly half of the dPAG neurons were classified as arm-modulated cells (49%, with 26% closed- and 23% open-modulated cells).
source: Based on the distribution of cells per arm score, roughly half of the dPAG neurons were classified as arm-modulated cells (49%, with 26% closed- and 23% open-modulated cells) (Figure 1H)
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from cell classification analysis.

claim: Two major, non-overlapping populations of dPAG neurons showed opposite changes in activity levels during transitions between arms.
source: During transitions between arms, we identified opposite changes in activity levels of these two major, non-overlapping populations of dPAG neurons (Figure 1I and Figure 2A–B).
evidence: This is a finding from analysis of behavior-aligned neural activity.

claim: The closed arm-activated ensemble showed a decrease in activity when mice traversed from a closed arm to an open arm.
source: For example, the closed arm-activated ensemble showed a decrease in activity when mice traversed from a closed arm to an open arm.
evidence: This is a specific finding from behavior-aligned activity analysis.

claim: Open and closed cells showed increased and decreased activity, respectively, during exploratory head dip behavior.
source: Moreover, open and closed cells showed increased and decreased activity, respectively, during exploratory head dip behavior (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a finding from behavior-aligned activity analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Aggregate activity of dPAG cells in the EPM did not show significantly higher activity in the open arms.
source: Aggregate activity of dPAG cells in the EPM did not show significantly higher activity in the open arms, showing that in the entire population, the closed and open cell patterns counterbalance each other (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a finding from population-level analysis shown in a supplementary figure.

claim: 95% of dPAG cells showed relatively low correlations of speed and neural activity, between −0.17 and +0.2.
source: Importantly, 95% of dPAG cells showed relatively low correlations of speed and neural activity, between −0.17 and +0.2.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from correlation analysis.

claim: Arm-related activity preferences are not driven by variations in velocity.
source: These results suggest that arm-related activity preferences are not driven by variations in velocity (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the low correlation between speed and neural activity.

claim: Support vector machine (SVM) decoders trained on dPAG activity obtained significantly higher than chance performance in identifying whether the mouse was in an open or closed arm.
source: Indeed, upon training support vector machine (SVM) decoders on dPAG activity, we obtained significantly higher than chance performance in identifying whether the mouse was in an open or closed arm (Figure 2E, see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a finding from machine learning classification analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Distance from the center of the maze is related to a gradient of threat, with the highest threat levels at the end of the open arms.
source: Thus, we argue that distance from the center of the maze is related to a gradient of threat, with the highest threat levels at the end of the open arms.
evidence: This is an interpretation of EPM behavior based on vulnerability to threats.

claim: Mice avoid the extreme end of the open arm more robustly than the beginning of the open arm.
source: The animal's behavior supports this view, as mice avoid the extreme end of the open arm more robustly than the beginning of the open arm (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a behavioral finding shown in a supplementary figure.

claim: A linear regression model showed significantly higher than chance performance in predicting EPM location index from dPAG cell activity.
source: We then fitted a linear regression model to predict the EPM location index from dPAG cell activity. Interestingly, the model showed significantly higher than chance performance in predicting EPM location index, suggesting that the identified dPAG ensembles may not only encode arm type, but rather a risk perception and threat exposure gradient (Figure 2F–G and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a finding from regression analysis shown in figures.

claim: The identified dPAG ensembles may encode a risk perception and threat exposure gradient rather than just arm type.
source: Interestingly, the model showed significantly higher than chance performance in predicting EPM location index, suggesting that the identified dPAG ensembles may not only encode arm type, but rather a risk perception and threat exposure gradient (Figure 2F–G and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the regression analysis results.

claim: Mice spent most of the trial away from the rat during predator exposure.
source: Mice spent most of the trial away from the rat (Figure 3A), indicating aversion from perceived threat.
evidence: This is a behavioral observation reported in the text and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Mice presented defensive strategy repertoires composed of approach and avoidance-related behaviors during rat exposure.
source: Consistent with previous threat imminence theories and the array of defensive behaviors evoked in the presence of a predator (Blanchard et al., 2011; McNaughton and Corr, 2004; Perusini and Fanselow, 2015; Stankowich, 2019), mice presented defensive strategy repertoires composed of approach and avoidance-related behaviors (i.e., escape and freeze) (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a behavioral observation supported by citations to prior theories.

claim: Freeze bouts lasted 2.1 ± 1.3 s on average during rat exposure.
source: Freeze bouts lasted 2.1 ± 1.3 s on average.
evidence: This is a quantitative behavioral measurement.

claim: Average dPAG activity increased with rat proximity, rat movement onset, and escape.
source: Notably, average dPAG activity increased with rat proximity, rat movement onset, and escape, and decreased during approach, while no significant change was observed during freezing (Figure 3C–E).
evidence: This is a finding from neural activity analysis shown in Figure 3C-E.

claim: Average dPAG activity decreased during approach to the rat.
source: Notably, average dPAG activity increased with rat proximity, rat movement onset, and escape, and decreased during approach, while no significant change was observed during freezing (Figure 3C–E).
evidence: This is a finding from neural activity analysis shown in Figure 3C-E.

claim: No significant change in average dPAG activity was observed during freezing.
source: Notably, average dPAG activity increased with rat proximity, rat movement onset, and escape, and decreased during approach, while no significant change was observed during freezing (Figure 3C–E).
evidence: This is a finding from neural activity analysis shown in Figure 3C-E.

claim: Mice displayed no signs of aversion nor differences in dPAG activity with proximity to a toy rat.
source: Importantly, mice displayed no signs of aversion nor differences in dPAG activity with proximity to a toy rat (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a control experiment result shown in a supplementary figure.

claim: Open cells showed higher activation than closed cells near the rat even though all cell types were positively activated.
source: Indeed, open cells showed higher activation than closed cells near the rat even though all cell types were positively activated (Figure 3F–H and Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a finding from ensemble-specific activity analysis shown in figures.

claim: Proximity to a live predator activated the neither cell ensemble.
source: The present results also showed that proximity to a live predator activated the neither cell ensemble.
evidence: This is a finding from neural activity analysis.

claim: The neither cell ensemble may require a higher degree of threat to be activated relative to open cells.
source: As the relatively low threat open arms did not significantly activate it, this ensemble of neurons may require a higher degree of threat to be activated relative to open cells.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing activation patterns across threat contexts.

claim: Closed cells showed increased activity following onset of both escape and freeze, despite these behaviors having opposite motor outputs.
source: Closed cells showed increased activity following onset of both escape and freeze, despite these behaviors having opposite motor outputs (Figure 3I–K).
evidence: This is a finding from behavior-aligned activity analysis shown in Figure 3I-K.

claim: Open and closed ensembles showed opposite activity patterns during freezing and approach onset even though these behaviors occur similarly far from the rat.
source: Additionally, even though freezing and approach onset occur similarly far from the rat (Figure 3A), open and closed ensembles showed opposite activity patterns and different generalized linear model (GLM) weights (Figure 3I–K).
evidence: This is a finding from comparing activity patterns and GLM analysis.

claim: Rat movement onset likely constitutes a threat signal and switches states from approach to avoidance.
source: Rat movement onset likely constitutes a threat signal and switches states from approach to avoidance, as predator movement is indicative of increased threat imminence.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on threat imminence theory.

claim: Rat movement is a significant predictor variable for less frequent approach and more occurrences of threat avoidance-related behaviors.
source: Indeed, rat movement is a significant predictor variable for less frequent approach and more occurrences of threat avoidance-related behaviors, such as escape and freezing (Figure 3—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This is a finding from GLM analysis shown in a supplementary figure.

claim: Rat movements are not consistently directed toward the mouse.
source: Interestingly, rat movement bouts are not consistently directed toward the mouse, as it most often increases distance toward the mouse (Figure 3—figure supplement 4B–C).
evidence: This is a finding from analysis of rat movement direction shown in supplementary figures.

claim: After rat movement onset, the threat avoidance-related closed arm ensembles displayed higher activity.
source: Accordingly, after rat movement onset, the threat avoidance-related closed arm ensembles displayed higher activity (Figure 3I–J).
evidence: This is a finding from behavior-aligned activity analysis shown in Figure 3I-J.

claim: dPAG cells used shared patterns of neural activity across rat and EPM assays to represent threat imminence.
source: Furthermore, dPAG cells also used shared patterns of neural activity across rat and EPM assays to represent threat imminence (measured as distance to threat) (Figure 3—figure supplement 5, see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a finding from CoCA analysis shown in a supplementary figure.

claim: dPAG neuronal activity can represent internal brain states using shared patterns of activity across different threats.
source: These results suggest that dPAG neuronal activity can represent internal brain states using shared patterns of activity across different threats.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cross-assay analysis results.

claim: Closed cells were more active during higher distance from threat and threat avoidance-related behaviors such as freezing and escaping.
source: Our results showed that closed cells were more active during higher distance from threat and threat avoidance-related behaviors, such as freezing and escaping, while open cells were more active during proximity to threats and exploratory head dips in the EPM (Figure 2 and Figure 3).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from multiple analyses shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Open cells were more active during proximity to threats and exploratory head dips in the EPM.
source: Our results showed that closed cells were more active during higher distance from threat and threat avoidance-related behaviors, such as freezing and escaping, while open cells were more active during proximity to threats and exploratory head dips in the EPM (Figure 2 and Figure 3).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from multiple analyses shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: dPAG closed and open cells were encoding threat avoidance and threat approach states, respectively.
source: The consistency of these results across behaviors and two different threat modalities indicates that dPAG closed and open cells were encoding threat avoidance and threat approach states, respectively.
evidence: This is an interpretation drawn from the consistency of findings across contexts.

claim: k-means clustering identified two clusters for EPM and three for the rat assay as optimal based on the Akaike information criterion.
source: We used the Akaike information criterion (AIC) to determine the optimal number of clusters for each assay, which were two clusters for EPM and three for the rat assay (see the Materials and methods section entitled 'k-Means clustering of neural data'; see also AIC values for a range of cluster numbers in Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from unsupervised clustering analysis with reference to a supplementary figure.

claim: Experimentally observed approach and avoidance clusters respectively had higher and lower scores than sampling distributions obtained from permuted behavioral labels.
source: Experimentally observed approach and avoidance clusters respectively had higher and lower scores than sampling distributions obtained from permuted behavioral labels, showing that our k-means approach identified activity patterns that strongly encode the avoidance/approach score (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a finding from statistical comparison of observed vs. shuffled data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Approach and avoidance clusters trained on one assay and applied on the other assay result in significantly different scores.
source: Lastly, we show that approach and avoidance clusters trained on one assay and applied on the other assay result in significantly different scores, despite the two assays having different geometries and distinct threat modalities (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a finding from cross-assay generalization analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: These results were not found when computing approach and avoidance cluster centroids defined on the control toy rat assay but applied to the rat assay.
source: Importantly, these results were not found when computing approach and avoidance cluster centroids defined on the control toy rat assay but applied to the rat assay (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a control analysis result shown in a supplementary figure.

claim: Approach and avoidance states are encoded using shared patterns of neural activity across assays.
source: These results indicate, using an unsupervised method, that approach and avoidance states are encoded using shared patterns of neural activity across assays.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the k-means clustering results.

claim: Similar results were obtained by employing a hidden Markov model (HMM).
source: Similar results were also obtained by employing a hidden Markov model (HMM), showing that the results in Figure 4 can be found using a diversity of computational approaches (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a finding from an alternative computational analysis shown in a supplementary figure.

claim: dPAG activity reflects moment-to-moment changes in the behavioral states of the animal.
source: Importantly, dPAG activity reflects moment-to-moment changes in the behavioral states of the animal.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the dynamic activity patterns observed.

claim: dPAG activity patterns may indicate threat perception rather than merely encoding defensive behavior movements.
source: Rather than merely encoding the defensive behavior movements, these activity patterns may indicate threat perception.
evidence: This is an interpretation of what the neural activity represents.

claim: Encoding of exploratory and defensive behavior has been reported in the amygdala.
source: Encoding of exploratory and defensive behavior has also been reported in the amygdala (Gründemann et al., 2019), indicating that multiple defensive nodes represent such brain states.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work on the amygdala.

claim: Multiple defensive nodes represent approach and avoidance brain states.
source: Encoding of exploratory and defensive behavior has also been reported in the amygdala (Gründemann et al., 2019), indicating that multiple defensive nodes represent such brain states.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing findings across brain regions.

claim: Rat approach and open arm exploration were correlated across mice.
source: Rat approach and open arm exploration were correlated across mice, indicating that these measures also reflected trait avoidance levels (Figure 4—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This is a finding from correlation analysis shown in a supplementary figure.

claim: Mice with a higher proportion of open cells in relation to closed cells displayed increased avoidance of open arms and rat.
source: We then found that mice with a higher proportion of open cells in relation to closed cells displayed increased avoidance of open arms and rat (Figure 4—figure supplement 4B–C).
evidence: This is a finding from correlation analysis shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Mice with more open arm cells display an increased sensitivity to risk evaluation reflected on increased avoidance of threat.
source: Considering this hypothesis, our results suggest that mice with more open arm cells display an increased sensitivity to risk evaluation reflected on increased avoidance of threat.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the correlation between ensemble composition and behavior.

claim: dPAG ensembles composition may integrate risk evaluation processes and influence individual mouse differences in threat avoidance traits.
source: These data indicate that in addition to encoding moment-to-moment changes in behavioral state, dPAG ensembles composition may integrate risk evaluation processes and influence individual mouse differences in threat avoidance traits.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the correlation between ensemble composition and individual differences.

claim: The dPAG's role in defense has been described as restricted to the initiation of escape.
source: The dPAG's role in defense has been described as restricted to the initiation of escape (Evans et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a characterization of prior work supported by a citation.

claim: A proposed model is that excitatory neurons initiate escape (but not other defensive behaviors) in response to imminent threat.
source: A proposed model is that excitatory neurons initiate escape (but not other defensive behaviors) in response to imminent threat (Evans et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a description of a model from prior work supported by a citation.

claim: Optogenetically stimulating vglut2-positive cells in dPAG caused escape.
source: Accordingly, optogenetically stimulating vglut2-positive cells in dPAG caused escape and presenting looming stimuli while optogenetically inhibiting those cells caused freezing (Evans et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a finding from prior work supported by a citation.

claim: Presenting looming stimuli while optogenetically inhibiting vglut2-positive dPAG cells caused freezing.
source: Accordingly, optogenetically stimulating vglut2-positive cells in dPAG caused escape and presenting looming stimuli while optogenetically inhibiting those cells caused freezing (Evans et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a finding from prior work supported by a citation.

claim: Recent data indicate that the dPAG's influence on defense is not restricted to escape initiation.
source: However, recent data indicate that the dPAG's influence on defense is not restricted to escape initiation.
evidence: This is a statement about recent findings that challenge the prior model.

claim: Optogenetic activation of dPAG CaMKIIα-positive neurons can cause both escape and freezing.
source: For example, optogenetic activation of dPAG CaMKIIα-positive neurons can cause both escape and freezing (Deng et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a finding from prior work supported by a citation.

claim: Increasing the optogenetic stimulation frequency of CaMKIIα-positive dPAG neurons switches responses from freezing to escape.
source: Increasing the optogenetic stimulation frequency of CaMKIIα-positive dPAG neurons switches responses from freezing to escape (Deng et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a finding from prior work supported by a citation.

claim: Activation of excitatory ventromedial hypothalamus projections to the dPAG induces freezing.
source: Supporting the view that the dPAG may promote freezing, activation of excitatory ventromedial hypothalamus projections to the dPAG induces freezing (Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a finding from prior work supported by a citation.

claim: The hypothalamic dorsal premammillary nucleus projections to the dPAG control escape elicited by numerous innate threats.
source: Conversely, the hypothalamic dorsal premammillary nucleus projections to the dPAG control escape elicited by numerous innate threats (Wang et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a finding from prior work supported by a citation.

claim: The medial prefrontal cortex promotes aversion and might regulate defensive strategies through projections to the dPAG.
source: Recent work shows that the medial prefrontal cortex promotes aversion and might regulate defensive strategies through projections to the dPAG (Vander Weele et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a finding from prior work supported by a citation.

claim: Through different inputs, the dPAG may integrate distinct aspects of emotional states, detect diverse threats, and coordinate a range of defensive responses, including freezing and escape.
source: These findings indicate that through different inputs, the dPAG may integrate distinct aspects of emotional states, detect diverse threats, and coordinate a range of defensive responses, including freezing and escape.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited literature on dPAG connectivity and function.

claim: When the subject can voluntarily approach the threat, the dPAG has a broader function in threat processing as a risk estimator that represents approach- and avoidance-related states.
source: We propose that when the subject can voluntarily approach the threat, the dPAG has a broader function in threat processing. It may then function as a risk estimator that represents approach- and avoidance-related states, and consequently influences a wide range of behaviors related to both approach and avoidance.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the current study's findings.

claim: dPAG cells differentiated between open and closed spaces in the EPM.
source: Our study reveals novel features of dPAG neurons. First, dPAG cells differentiated between open and closed spaces in the EPM.
evidence: This is a summary of a key finding from the study.

claim: Closed cell activity patterns were positively correlated with threat perception represented by the predator's movement.
source: Second, we show that closed cell activity patterns were positively correlated with threat perception represented by the predator's movement.
evidence: This is a summary of a key finding from the study.

claim: Escape and freezing correlated with increased closed cell activity despite having opposite motor outputs.
source: Furthermore, despite having opposite motor outputs, escape and freezing correlated with increased closed cell activity.
evidence: This is a summary of a key finding from the study.

claim: Open cell activity was inversely correlated with distance to threat.
source: Conversely, open cell activity was inversely correlated with distance to threat.
evidence: This is a summary of a key finding from the study.

claim: Open cell activity starts decreasing following escape onset, while closed cell activity increases after flight initiation.
source: However, open cell activity starts decreasing following escape onset, while closed cell activity increases after flight initiation (Figure 3J).
evidence: This is a finding about activity dynamics shown in Figure 3J.

claim: dPAG is not simply a premotor area but rather reflects the subjects' underlying emotional state.
source: Our observations suggest that dPAG is not simply a premotor area but rather reflects the subjects' underlying emotional state, in agreement with previous work (Carvalho et al., 2015; Carvalho et al., 2018; Johansen et al., 2010; Kim et al., 2013; Kincheski et al., 2012; Nashold et al., 1969).
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by the current findings and citations to prior work.

claim: dPAG activity represented location within the EPM.
source: This idea is consistent with the fact that dPAG activity represented location within the EPM (Figure 2F)
evidence: This is a finding from regression analysis shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The dPAG used shared patterns of neural activity across rat and EPM assays to represent threat imminence.
source: and that the dPAG used shared patterns of neural activity across rat and EPM assays to represent threat imminence (Figure 3—figure supplement 5)
evidence: This is a finding from CoCA analysis shown in a supplementary figure.

claim: The finding that the dPAG uses a conserved representation of threat approach and avoidance across assays expands prior results using stimulation, calcium imaging, electrophysiology, and c-fos expression.
source: The finding that the dPAG uses a conserved representation of threat approach and avoidance across assays expands prior results using stimulation, calcium imaging, electrophysiology, and c-fos expression (Bittencourt et al., 2005; Brandão et al., 1982; Canteras and Goto, 1999; Deng et al., 2016; Esteban Masferrer et al., 2020; Evans et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a statement about how the current findings relate to and extend prior work, supported by citations.

claim: A role beyond motor output execution has been proposed for the ventral PAG, as its neural activity reflects threat probability associated with specific cues.
source: A role beyond motor output execution has also been proposed for the ventral PAG, as its neural activity reflects threat probability associated with specific cues (Wright and McDannald, 2019; Wright et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a finding from prior work on ventral PAG supported by citations.

claim: Based on its connectivity, the dPAG is well positioned to have a privileged role in computing threat imminence and threat probability.
source: Based on its connectivity, the dPAG is well positioned to have a privileged role in computing threat imminence and threat probability, as it receives input from sensory, limbic, and cognitive areas (Silva and McNaughton, 2019), and projects not only to centers that control motor actions (Ferreira-Pinto et al., 2018; Marchand and Hagino, 1983) but also to prosencephalic targets likely to mediate fear behavior (Gross and Canteras, 2012; Krout and Loewy, 2000; Motta et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an inference about dPAG function based on its anatomical connectivity, supported by citations.

claim: The dPAG receives input from sensory, limbic, and cognitive areas.
source: Based on its connectivity, the dPAG is well positioned to have a privileged role in computing threat imminence and threat probability, as it receives input from sensory, limbic, and cognitive areas (Silva and McNaughton, 2019)
evidence: This is an anatomical fact supported by a citation.

claim: The dPAG projects to centers that control motor actions.
source: and projects not only to centers that control motor actions (Ferreira-Pinto et al., 2018; Marchand and Hagino, 1983)
evidence: This is an anatomical fact supported by citations.

claim: The dPAG projects to prosencephalic targets likely to mediate fear behavior.
source: but also to prosencephalic targets likely to mediate fear behavior (Gross and Canteras, 2012; Krout and Loewy, 2000; Motta et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an anatomical fact supported by citations.

claim: The study reveals two large functional neuronal ensembles of the dPAG representing internal states.
source: In summary, our study reveals two large functional neuronal ensembles of the dPAG representing internal states.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding of the study.

claim: dPAG cells are not only encoding specific behaviors or threat imminence but also dPAG ensemble activity reflects moment-to-moment changes in the approach-avoidance state of the animal.
